questions.q: You call totals.sort() on an array of order totals in naira, with no comparator. What rule does it use?
questions.explain: Without a comparator, sort compares string forms, so "1200000" comes before "25000" because "1" is before "2". For numbers always pass (a, b) => a - b.
options: It sorts numbers from smallest to largest
It converts every item to a string and orders the strings character by character
It sorts by the order the numbers were added
It throws, because numbers need a comparator

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The strings "100", "1000", "25", "3" are ordered by their first characters: "1" before "2" before "3". "100" is a prefix of "1000", so it comes first.

questions.q: A comparator compare(a, b) should say that b must come before a. What must it return?
questions.explain: Negative means a first, positive means a after b (so b first), zero means equal. That is why b - a gives a descending order.
options: A negative number
A positive number
Zero
false

questions.q: A colleague writes prices.sort((a, b) => a > b). What is wrong with it?
questions.explain: true becomes 1 and false becomes 0. The comparator can say "after" or "equal" but never "before", which breaks its contract. No error is thrown; the array just comes back in a wrong order. Use a - b.
options: Nothing: true and false are converted to the right numbers
It sorts in descending order instead of ascending
It returns 1 or 0 and never a negative number, so the sort is never told that one item comes before another; the result depends on the engine and may be unsorted
It throws a TypeError because a comparator must return a number

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: sort rearranges the array in place and returns the same array. cheapestFirst and prices are one array, so both the sorting and the push show up in prices. toSorted would have made a copy.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: toSorted returns a new sorted array and leaves the original alone. b - a puts larger numbers first.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: < compares character codes, and every capital letter has a smaller code than every lower-case letter. localeCompare uses language rules, so case does not split the list in two.
options:
Bola Chioma ada tunde
ada Bola Chioma tunde

ada Bola Chioma tunde
ada Bola Chioma tunde

Bola Chioma ada tunde
Bola Chioma ada tunde

ada tunde Bola Chioma
ada Bola Chioma tunde

questions.q: Bubble sort is fast when a large item is out of place near the front, but slow when a small item is out of place near the end. Why?
questions.explain: A pass keeps swapping the same large item forward until it meets a larger one. A small item near the end is swapped back only once per pass. Insertion sort does not have this weakness: it slides an item left as far as it needs in one step.
options: Because it compares items from right to left
One pass can carry a large item many places towards the end, but moves a small item only one place towards the front, so it needs one pass per place
Because small items are compared more often than large ones
Because the early-exit flag only works for large items

questions.q: This bubble sort counts its passes. What does it print?
questions.explain: For [1, 2, 3, 5, 4], pass 1 swaps 5 and 4, and pass 2 finds nothing to swap and stops. For [2, 3, 4, 5, 1] the 1 moves only one place left per pass, so it needs 4 passes (the loop ends before a fifth, empty pass is needed).

questions.q: How many comparisons does selection sort make on an array of 100 items that is already sorted?
questions.explain: Selection sort must scan the whole unsorted part to be sure it found the minimum, whatever the input: 99 + 98 + … + 1 = 100 × 99 / 2 = 4,950. It is Θ(n²) in every case.

questions.q: When could selection sort be a reasonable choice despite its n²/2 comparisons?
questions.explain: Selection sort makes at most n − 1 swaps. If each write is costly (large records, worn-out flash memory), that can outweigh its comparisons for small n. For nearly sorted data insertion sort is better, and selection sort is not stable.
options: When the data is nearly sorted
When you need a stable sort
When the list is small and moving an item is far more expensive than comparing two items, because it does at most one swap per position
When the list has millions of items

questions.q: A leaderboard of 5,000 customers is sorted by points. One customer's points just increased and the board must be re-sorted. Which of these sorts does the least work?
questions.explain: Insertion sort does about one comparison per item plus one per place the changed customer moves: roughly n. Selection sort still does n²/2, quick sort with a last-item pivot is quadratic on sorted data, bubble sort needs one pass per place the customer moves towards the front, and merge sort does about n log₂ n / 2 even on sorted data.
options: Selection sort
Insertion sort
Quick sort with the last item as the pivot
Bubble sort, because it has an early exit
Merge sort, because it is always O(n log n)

questions.q: An inversion is a pair of items in the wrong order relative to each other. How many does [3, 1, 2, 5, 4] have, and so how many shifts does insertion sort make on it?
questions.explain: The pairs in the wrong order are (3, 1), (3, 2) and (5, 4). Insertion sort shifts one item per inversion, so it makes 3 shifts. A sorted array has 0 inversions, a reversed one n(n − 1)/2.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: On sorted input each new item is compared once with its left neighbour and stays: n − 1 = 4. On reversed input every item slides all the way to the front: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 comparisons, n(n − 1)/2.

questions.q: In merge(left, right), when the two front items compare equal, the code takes the item from left. What does that decision give you?
questions.explain: The left half holds the items that came earlier in the input. Taking from the left on a tie keeps equal items in input order. Taking from the right (<= 0 instead of < 0) still sorts correctly but loses stability.
options: Fewer comparisons
Stability: equal items keep their original order, which is what makes merge sort stable
Protection against unsorted inputs
Nothing; taking from the right would be exactly the same

questions.q: Orders are tagged with the branch they came from. What does this merge print?
questions.explain: At time 10 the right item is not strictly smaller than the left one, so the left (Lagos) order goes first. When Lagos runs out, the rest of Abuja is appended without comparing.
options: 8A 9L 10L 12A

questions.q: Merge sort is O(n log n) for every input. What does it cost that quick sort does not?
questions.explain: Merging writes into a new array, so merge sort needs memory proportional to n. Quick sort partitions in place and only needs the recursion stack, O(log n) on average.
options: O(n²) comparisons on sorted input
O(n) extra memory for the merged arrays
It is not stable
It needs the input to be numbers

questions.q: Why does merge sort make about n log₂ n comparisons?
questions.explain: An array of n items can be halved about log₂ n times before the pieces have one item. On every level, the merges together process all n items once. n work times log₂ n levels is O(n log n).
options: Each item is compared with every other item log n times
Halving gives about log₂ n levels, and all the merges on one level together touch each item once, so each level costs about n
The merge step is O(log n) and it runs n times
It sorts log n items at a time

questions.q: A quick sort always picks the last item of the range as its pivot. Why is it O(n²) on data that is already sorted?
questions.explain: A good pivot splits the range into two similar halves (log n levels). The largest item splits it into n − 1 and 0, so there are n levels costing n, n − 1, n − 2, … comparisons: about n²/2. The recursion also gets n calls deep.
options: Because sorted data has many duplicates
The last item is the largest, so each partition puts everything on one side and removes only the pivot, giving n levels of work
Because the partition swaps every item on every level
It is not: quick sort is always O(n log n)

questions.q: What does choosing the pivot at random change?
questions.explain: With a fixed pivot rule, some inputs (such as sorted data) are always bad. With a random pivot, badness depends on the coin flips, not on the input. The worst case is still possible in theory, but vanishingly unlikely for large arrays.
options: It makes quick sort stable
It makes the worst case O(n log n)
No particular input is bad any more; the expected cost is O(n log n) on every input, and a quadratic run needs extremely bad luck
It removes the need for recursion

questions.q: This is one Lomuto partition step with the last item as the pivot. What does it print?
questions.explain: 2 and 4 are smaller than 5 and are swapped to the front, leaving [2, 4, 9, 7, 5] with store = 2. The final swap puts the pivot 5 at index 2, exchanging it with 9. Everything left of index 2 is smaller, everything right of it is larger; the right side is not necessarily sorted (here it happens to be).
options: 2 4 5 7 9 pivot at 2
2 4 5 9 7 pivot at 2
2 4 9 7 5 pivot at 4
2 4 7 9 5 pivot at 2

questions.q: You sort 50,000 order lines by status, which has only four possible values. A two-way quick sort with a random pivot is very slow. Why, and what fixes it?
questions.explain: Once a range contains only one status, a two-way partition behaves like sorted input: O(n²). Three-way partitioning groups the equal items around the pivot and never recurses into them.
options: Random pivots do not work on strings; use a numeric key
Items equal to the pivot all go to one side, so ranges full of equal items shrink by one per level; a three-way partition (smaller, equal, larger) finishes all equal items in one pass
The comparator is too slow; cache the status
Quick sort cannot sort fewer than five distinct values

questions.q: Why can no sort that only compares pairs of items beat O(n log n) in the worst case?
questions.explain: The sort must be able to tell all n! arrangements apart. With yes/no answers, k comparisons distinguish at most 2k cases, so k must be at least log₂(n!), which is about n log₂ n. Sorts that do not compare, like counting sort, are not bound by this.
options: Because the fastest computers can only do n log n operations per second
n items have n! possible orders, each comparison has two outcomes and can at best halve the possibilities, and log₂(n!) grows like n log₂ n
Because every item must be compared with every other item
Because recursion always adds a log n factor

questions.q: You must order 2 million product reviews by star rating (1 to 5). What is the fastest reasonable approach?
questions.explain: When keys are small whole numbers known in advance, you do not need comparisons at all. One pass counts (or groups) the reviews per rating, and a second writes them out. Grouping into five lists in input order is also stable.
options: Merge sort, because it is optimal
Insertion sort, because there are few distinct values
Count the reviews per rating and write them out group by group (counting sort): O(n + k) with k = 5
Quick sort with the last item as the pivot

questions.q: What does it mean that a sort is stable?
questions.explain: Stability is about ties. If two orders have the same date and you sort by date, a stable sort keeps them in the order they were in before. Not changing the input is a different property (copying, like toSorted).
options: It never throws an error
It gives the same running time on every input
Items that compare as equal keep the relative order they had in the input
It does not change the input array

questions.q: You want orders grouped by date, and within each date the largest amount first, using two sorts with a stable sort. In which order do you sort?
questions.explain: The last sort decides the main grouping, so it must be by date. Because it is stable, orders with equal dates keep the order the first sort gave them: by amount. Sort by the least important key first.
options: By date first, then by amount
By amount (descending) first, then by date
The order does not matter with a stable sort
It cannot be done with two sorts

questions.q: Tasks arrive in the order shown. What does this print?
questions.explain: toSorted and sort are guaranteed stable since ES2019. Tasks with the same priority stay in arrival order: invoice #3 before invoice #4, refund #7 before email #9.
options: invoice #3, invoice #4, refund #7, email #9, backup
invoice #4, invoice #3, email #9, refund #7, backup
invoice #3, invoice #4, email #9, refund #7, backup
backup, email #9, refund #7, invoice #4, invoice #3

questions.q: A developer tries to sort by city and then by points (highest first), but writes && instead of ||. What does it print?
questions.explain: With &&, a tie on city (0) returns 0 immediately, so customers in the same city are never ordered by points and keep their input order. For different cities it returns the points comparison instead of the city comparison, which here puts Lagos first. || means "use the next key only when this one is a tie".
options: Tunde Chioma Bola Musa
Musa Bola Chioma Tunde
Bola Musa Tunde Chioma
Chioma Musa Tunde Bola

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 1 September comes first. Orders 1 and 2 tie on date and amount, so the id decides: 1 then 2. On 2 September the larger amount (order 3, ₦9,000) comes before order 4. The unique id as a final key makes the result independent of stability.

questions.q: An API returns orders 20 per page, sorted by created_at. Many orders share the same timestamp. Some customers report an order appearing on two pages and another on none. What is the fix?
questions.explain: With ties, the database may order equal rows differently on each request, so page boundaries move. A unique tie-breaker such as ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC gives exactly one possible order.
options: Use a stable sorting algorithm in the API
Increase the page size
Add a unique column (such as the id) as a final sort key, so the order is total and every request agrees on it
Sort in JavaScript instead of in the database

questions.q: Inside a function render(products) you need the products by price. The array was passed in by the caller. What should you use?
questions.explain: sort would rearrange an array that belongs to someone else, a surprising side effect. toSorted returns a sorted copy. Both are stable.
options: products.sort(byPrice), because it is faster
products.toSorted(byPrice), because it leaves the caller's array unchanged
Either; they do the same thing
A for loop, because built-in sorts are not stable

questions.q: V8's Array.prototype.sort uses TimSort, a mix of merge sort and insertion sort. How many comparisons does it need on 10,000 items that are already sorted?
questions.explain: TimSort scans for runs that are already ordered. A sorted array is one run, found with n − 1 comparisons, and there is nothing to merge. On random data it falls back to O(n log n) merging.
options: About 10,000 × log₂ 10,000, like any merge sort
About 10,000: it detects one run that is already in order
Zero: it checks a "sorted" flag on the array

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: undefined items are always moved to the end, and the comparator is never called with them, whatever direction you sort in. The numbers are sorted descending by b - a.
questions.code:
const cart = [3500, undefined, 800, 1200];
console.log(cart.toSorted((a, b) => b - a).map(String).join(" "));
options: 3500 1200 800 undefined
undefined 3500 1200 800
3500 undefined 1200 800
800 1200 3500 undefined

questions.q: One product in a catalogue has price: NaN because of a bad import. What happens when you sort by (a, b) => a.price - b.price?
questions.explain: Only undefined gets special treatment. NaN - 5 is NaN, which is not negative or positive, so the NaN item looks equal to everything; that breaks consistency, and other items can end up in the wrong order. Validate data before sorting.
options: The NaN product is moved to the end, like undefined
The sort throws a RangeError
Every comparison with it returns NaN, which the sort treats as "equal", so the result can be out of order around it without any error
NaN is treated as 0

questions.q: A dashboard shows the 10 largest orders out of 3 million. What is the best approach in JavaScript if the data is already in memory?
questions.explain: A full sort is O(n log n) to keep ten items. A size-10 min-heap holds the current top ten, and each order is compared with the smallest of them: effectively linear. Ten passes of bubble or selection sort would also work, but cost 10n comparisons with a heavier constant, and grow badly if the dashboard later wants the top 1,000.
options: Sort all 3 million by amount and take the first 10
Keep a min-heap of size 10 while scanning once: O(n log 10)
Run bubble sort for 10 passes
Use selection sort for 10 steps

questions.q: An endpoint loads 200,000 orders from PostgreSQL, sorts them in Node by date and returns the newest 20. What is the better design?
questions.explain: With an index on the sort columns, the database already has the rows in order and stops after 20. Moving 200,000 rows into Node to throw away 199,980 costs network, memory and CPU on every request.
options: Use merge sort instead of the built-in sort
Cache the sorted array in memory forever
Ask the database for ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20, backed by an index, so it reads only the rows it returns
Sort in the browser instead

questions.q: A comparator parses two date strings with new Date(...) on every call. Sorting 100,000 orders is slow. Why, and what helps?
questions.explain: A comparison sort calls the comparator O(n log n) times, so any work inside it is multiplied. Precomputing the key (for example Date.parse once per order) turns millions of parses into 100,000.
options: Dates cannot be sorted; use strings
The comparator runs about n log₂ n times (well over a million), parsing two dates each time; compute a numeric key once per order, then sort by the key
The sort is O(n²) because of the dates
Parsing only happens once, so it is not the cause

questions.q: Write insertionSort(items, compare) that returns a sorted copy of items using insertion sort (take the next item and slide it left past every item that is larger). It should print 800 1200 3500 3500 99000 and then 4500 1200 800 (the original, unchanged).
questions.explain: Copy first, so the caller's array is untouched. The inner loop shifts larger items one place right and stops at the first item that is not larger (> 0, not >= 0, which keeps equal items in order and makes the sort stable).

questions.q: Write merge(a, b) that merges two arrays of order times, each sorted ascending, into one sorted array in O(n + m). It should print 08:55 09:02 10:15 10:15 11:30 13:40 and then 09:00 09:30.
questions.explain: Compare the two fronts and take the earlier; on a tie take from a (stable). When one array runs out, copy the rest of the other: it is already sorted and later than everything taken. Fixed-width HH:MM strings compare correctly with <.

questions.q:
Sort the products by category A to Z, and within a category by price, most expensive first. Use one comparator with toSorted. It should print:

drinks 1500 Zobo
drinks 800 Water
food 12000 Rice 5kg
food 3500 Garri
home 4500 Bucket
questions.explain: The first key decides unless it returns 0; || then falls through to the second key. b.price - a.price puts higher prices first.
questions.expected:
drinks 1500 Zobo
drinks 800 Water
food 12000 Rice 5kg
food 3500 Garri
home 4500 Bucket

questions.q: Write selectionSort(items) for numbers that returns { sorted, swaps }, where swaps counts the swaps it actually made (skip the swap when the minimum is already in place). It should print 1 2 3 4 5 swaps: 1 and 1 2 3 swaps: 0.
questions.explain: For [3, 2, 1, 4, 5] the first step swaps 3 and 1, which also puts 2 in place, so only one swap is needed. Selection sort never makes more than n − 1 swaps, but it always makes n(n − 1)/2 comparisons.

questions.q: Write countInversions(items) that counts the pairs i < j with items[i] > items[j]. It tells you how far from sorted a leaderboard is (and exactly how many shifts insertion sort will make). A simple O(n²) double loop is fine. It should print 0 3 10.
questions.explain: Check every pair once. A reversed array of n items has n(n − 1)/2 inversions, the maximum. A modified merge sort can count inversions in O(n log n): each time merge takes from the right, every item still waiting on the left forms an inversion with it.

questions.q: Sort reviews by star rating (1 to 5), highest first, without a comparator: group them into one list per rating in a single pass, then output the lists from 5 down to 1. Keep reviews with the same rating in their input order. It should print r2:5 r5:5 r1:4 r4:3 r3:1 r6:1.
questions.explain: This is counting sort (in its "bucket per key" form). It never compares two reviews, so the n log n lower bound does not apply: one pass to group, one to output, O(n + k) for k ratings. Pushing in input order makes it stable.

questions.q: Tests for a sort need a helper. Write isSorted(items, compare) that returns true when every item is not after the next one. It should print true true false true.
questions.explain: Checking neighbours is enough, because a consistent comparator is transitive. Equal neighbours are allowed (> 0, not >= 0). An empty or one-item array is sorted. Remember that isSorted alone is not a full test: an output of [] is sorted too, so also compare the contents with the input.

questions.q: Put order statuses in workflow order, paid then shipped then delivered, in place and in one pass, using a three-way partition around shipped (keep a boundary for the paid region at the front and one for the delivered region at the back). It should print paid paid shipped shipped delivered delivered delivered.
questions.explain: This is the three-way partition from quick sort (also called the Dutch national flag problem). After swapping a delivered item to the back, i does not advance, because the item that came from the back has not been examined yet. Each step either advances i or shrinks gt, so it is one pass: O(n).
questions.expected: paid paid shipped shipped delivered delivered delivered
